speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And thank you for the opportunity to join this debate on the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As a practitioner in the industry, I wholeheartedly welcome these amendments and I would like to seek the following clarifications and make the following suggestions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As inspectors are given a degree of power and authority, what happens when such powers are abused?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It would be expected that these inspectors discharge their duties professionally and in a demeanour expected of any public officer.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I have encountered a variety of dishonest actors in the industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them are educators and a majority of them are agents.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Education institutions that engage agents may provide accurate information about a programme; however, there is little education institutions can do should such marketing agents go off script and use unethical means to close a sale.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly so as it is not realistic to expect all prospective students to be familiar with the prevailing rules and regulations in order to qualify them for funding support from the Government.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is incredibly upsetting to see marketing agents going to the heartlands using potentially inaccurate and misleading information to recruit students.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, am happy that this Bill also captures marketing agents.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: There should be no room for unscrupulous agents to profit from Government-funded training programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: A high standard of education is one of them.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The SkillsFuture programme has delivered in many ways to encourage Singaporeans to take charge of their learning and career development.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It promotes lifelong learning, ensuring the workforce in Singapore is equipped with the relevant skills to meet the changing economy, thereby facilitating Singaporeans to transition into new industries and occupations.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, care should be taken that funding should only be provided for students who genuinely wish to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to take the opportunity to respond to comments made by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim in his speech yesterday.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that even more so trainers of SkillsFuture and WSG courses should undergo appropriate training to teach.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I myself have undergone the Advanced Certificate of Training Assessment (ACTA) course which was a precursor to the ACLP programme which Assoc Prof Lim had referred to yesterday.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In my course of work, I have hired and observed many trainers and there is a difference between those who have and have not gone through the programme.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They are able to design a programme and the definition of teaching is the engagement of learners to enable understanding and application of knowledge, concepts and processes through design, content selection, delivery, assessment and reflection.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Also, the nature of such courses is competency-based, practical and vocational in nature and not necessarily academic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I often lean on my experience in sports and I know that the best athlete may not be the best coaches.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, if you are a practitioner, of course if you are great at what you do, you are able to impart passion and ignite a fire to it to enable your students, your charges, your athletes to go further and pursue this.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But let us be very clear, that when you are in the training ground, when you are at the pool or the court, you are there to teach, you are there to coach and having the right skills is of utmost importance.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the proposed amendments to the Bill will safeguard not just Singaporeans but the reputation and brand of Singapore and its training and education system.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The ongoing conflict in Ukraine, US-China tensions, China's trajectory as it recovers from COVID-19, the likelihood of recessions in US and EU, political instability in other countries and many more macroeconomic trends, cast uncertainties on the economy's prospects for the short-to-medium term.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite these uncertainties, there remains opportunities, provided we continue to stay united and demonstrate to the world that Singapore remains an open, safe, stable and reliable country and most importantly possess a capable and relevant workforce so that we can continue to attract investments and, as a result, have good jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That has been and continues to be Singapore's formula for success.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the global competition for investment is intensifying and we must continue to upskill and reskill ourselves to strengthen our value proposition and remain relevant to the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the short-to-medium term macroeconomic challenges, the need to upskill and reskill is nothing new for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has been integral for our success and will continue to be a cornerstone of our economic strategy as we continue to ensure that we remain relevant to the world by having the right skillsets that the world requires.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Education should be understood broadly and not stop prematurely at the end of a person's schooling life.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nor should education be defined solely within the confines of a school.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Continuous education must constantly prepare Singapore's workers for future workplace demands which is evolving very rapidly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am pleased that we remain committed to our Continuing Education and Training (CET) Masterplan and I am happy to hear from Minister Chan that our education system and MOE will "move beyond the first 15 years of education to the next 50 years" as mentioned in the Straits Times last Friday.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, MOE has extended its portfolio to include not only classroom learning, but more importantly, lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since the Skills Development Levy Act in 1979 and the establishment of Skill Development fund, we have shown and proved that in Singapore, we remain committed to training our workforce and have been improving and developing how we continuously train and upskill our workforce; including the passing of the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency Act 2016 which established the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency and the topping up of SkillsFuture credit during the COVID-19 period.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: SkillsFuture is a key enabler in developing the culture, infrastructure and platform for continuous education and learning.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: SkillsFuture also represents a repository of resource for our workforce to attain mastery of skills and it must remain so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Education must be more than just having the right paper qualification.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must strive to achieve excellence through continuous knowledge acquisition and application, and building relevant experience required in the industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For our workforce to continuously develop, attain skills mastery and remain nimble to take advantage of new opportunities and also to plug skills gap around the world, SkillsFuture must aspire to have the participation of as many people in our workforce as possible.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Worryingly, the percentage of people who use SFC is highest among those in their 30s and it reduces among those in their 40s and 50s and older.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And as we move towards increasing the participation rate in developing skills and improving the effectiveness and the value of training, the underlying process of disbursing grants, collecting levies and onboarding the support of trusted education and training partners must be simple to encourage participation yet robust to prevent any abuse.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I have three clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And lastly, how do we improve the training efficacy and assess SkillsFuture's success in meeting its strategic goals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Allow me to elaborate on these three points.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, the overpayments for SkillsFuture Singapore is attributed to errors in manual processing and SSG has shared that it is taking measures to reduce reliance on declarations and manual processing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And if not, what is the implementation plan?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Has SSG completed the process of recovering the outstanding SDL owed by companies and how do we prevent similar occurrences?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given this Bill will give SSG greater enforcement powers, will SSG be resourced with additional staff with the right skillset to implement effective enforcement?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also note that the Bill indicates extra financial expenditure, what is the expected increase in operating cost?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Based on data shared by Minister Chan in the November Sitting, what is more worrying is the decreased rate of participation as age increase.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there plans to encourage more of our mature workers to participate in upskilling and retraining?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Possibly, one opportunity is to encourage our mature workers to transit to a second career to be trainers and impart their experience to the rest of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, how do we increase the effectiveness of training for the courses supported by SkillsFuture?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On quality of training, I do note from the website that there are many training partners.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From just a search between "A" and "C" alone, there are already 60 training partners.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure the quality of training is preserved, to which I agree with what our fellow colleague Mr Mark Chay has mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the accreditation of the instructor, are the training partners regularly audited too?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On effectiveness of training, can SSG considering using outcome-based course subsidies?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we have a tiered course subsidy system where the full subsidy is only granted when the individual or organisation can show proof that they have implemented or applied what was learnt during the course.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, for the Implementing Lean Sigma course, which is a course on productivity, can the full subsidy be given only after the individual or company show that they have delivered projects to improve their productivity?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And on simplicity, there is a SSG website, SkillsFuture website, MySkillsFuture portal, SSG-WSG website.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As an end-user, the landscape can be very confusing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can this be simplified to be more customer-centric similar to the "Support-Go-Where" portal that provides the inter-agency support available for individuals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Skillsfuture is important in promoting lifelong learning amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we boost the participation rate from the current 30%?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As it is essential that older workers upgrade their skills, how can we encourage more mature workers to participate in the SkillsFuture programmes?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, how can we enhance the effectiveness of training in SkillsFuture courses?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must ensure that the quality of training is not affected, even as we increase the amount being offered.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am also aware that Singaporeans who wish to participate in these courses must visit various websites, such as SkillsFuture, My SkillsFuture, SSG-WSG sites, and this can cause some confusion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, SSG can consolidate these websites into one website such as the "Support-Go-Where" portal to facilitate participation in SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Notwithstanding the clarification above, I stand in support of the Bill to enhance the regulatory powers of SkillsFuture against fraud and abuse of its incentives and grants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Lifelong learning is now an integral part of our social compact in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through continuous education, our people are staying updated with the relevant knowledge and skillsets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This enables us to be competitive in employment and contribute meaningfully to our families and community.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SkillsFuture plays an important role in our Continuing Education and Training (CET) landscape.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In MySkillsFuture portal, these available courses and training providers are grouped by industries and areas of training.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Learners can register for courses and claim SkillsFuture Credits via this website.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most assume that the courses offered on this website have been vetted and are recognised by the Government.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, why would the Government permit Government funds to be used on these programmes?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we provide greater clarity on the validity and quality of these courses?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does the Ministry plan to make the portal even simpler and more straightforward, so that the public can check for accredited training providers easily?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are there any guidelines to help the training providers promote their programmes?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry exert greater control over where such courses are offered, in addition to the website?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, how will the Ministry familiarise Singaporeans with Industry Transformation Maps so that Singaporeans will know which relevant certified courses to enrol in?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When they turn up on the day of the courses, they are asked to click on a few buttons and leave the training venues shortly after signing the attendance sheets, without learning what the courses promised to offer.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In other words, does the Act prohibit the training providers from offering irrelevant items to attract course participants, even though such courses are funded by SSG?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have also received feedback about seniors being recruited to attend courses, especially the IT-related ones, even though they do not have the required language or foundation subject knowledge to understand the training materials.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do SSG's authorised inspectors and persons contact the participants and check on the learning outcomes?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does SSG check on the courses which are conducted virtually, if any?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such random checks will deter training providers from making fraudulent representations about participants passing courses when they had failed.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the Bill is passed, can the persons convicted of the offences be blacklisted and barred from setting up or financing other training operators for a minimum period of time?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does Government prevent scammers from posing as accredited training providers, which can be found on SkillsFuture's online portal and obtain personal information from potential applicants?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) are credible training providers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But are we relying too much on these IHLs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does the Government encourage credible professionals to become SkillsFuture's certified trainers?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Private sector players maybe more updated and relevant as they can be more nimble and quicker to customise programmes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Gone are the days when Universities were the main authority on one's qualifications for a job.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Tech companies must continue to drive movement where one's proficiency in a particular software leads to a new career opportunity.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Smaller training providers may be more flexible than the conventional IHLs when customising training syllabus.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can SkillsFuture work with the respective sector agencies, like the Singapore Accountancy Commission, to groom more individual trainers, like the Chartered Accountants, lawyers and engineers who will advertise their courses responsibly?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will create a centralised system and better support career development for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification on both Bills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the difficulty in determining the competencies, expertise or skills to be advanced by a course or programme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes advertising on the curriculum, modules or subjects to be covered or competencies, expertise or skills that will be advanced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are good faith reasons for why curriculum, modules or subjects to be covered may change after advertising for a course has started.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The subject matter may have evolved, or the curriculum may need to adapt to the interests and proficiency of the class.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The competencies, expertise or skills that a course actually succeeds in advancing may also be fairly subjective.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share if the Ministry intends to proactively monitor advertising by course providers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or will the Ministry rely on complaints by the public to identify potentially false or misleading advertisements before intervening?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister also share if the Ministry will provide guidance to course providers on best practices on advertising and in managing communications with participants especially on changes in course content to avoid any dispute over false advertising in the first place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on identifying fraudulent claims at an earlier stage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This follows the recommendations of an inter-agency task force set up to review SSG's fraud mitigation capabilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that it has been four years since these systems were introduced, can the Ministry share how it is monitoring the effectiveness of these fraud detection systems?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry also provide an update on how effective these systems have been?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is on the incorporation of a deferred payment model.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Lambda School in California teaches information technology skills online and charges no tuition fees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, students can agree to pay a percentage of their income after they are employed, and only if they are making more than US$50,000 a year in the first five years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The deal is that students pay back 17% of their income from their first two years of work after, if earnings exceed US$50,000 a year, with a cap of US$30,000 of fees they pay in total.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, students also have the option of paying US$20,000 in tuition upfront and keeping their future income.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the training institute does not impart transferable knowledge to trainees that results in a successful outcome, the institute will not benefit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, what are the Ministry's findings on the usefulness of such a model in Singapore Sir, notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have seen first-hand the transformative power of education and I believe that everyone should have the opportunity to continue learning and growing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is why I rise in support of the two Bills, which aim to strengthen the regulatory powers of SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) to prevent fraud and abuse of its incentives and funds but, above all, protect lifelong learners and their interests.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will help to deter training providers from trying to abuse SSG's incentives and funds and ensure that the money provided by SSG is being used in a way that supports lifelong learning and the growth of individuals.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will help ensure adequate oversight and accountability but, importantly, put errant training providers to task.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, there are a couple of concerns about the amendments.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This could lead to an unfair distribution of the burden of compliance and discourage small businesses and organisations from participating in SSG's programmes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Small businesses and organisations are vital for driving innovation and economic growth.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, it could indirectly impact students, such as reduced access to certain courses or programmes or increased cost.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Without adequate oversight and clear guidelines on how enforcement actions will be carried out, there is a risk that SSG's powers may be perceived as misused or abused.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This could lead to a lack of trust in the system and discourage people from participating in the SSG's programmes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To address these concerns, there are a few suggestions for the Ministry to consider.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The first would be to clarify the criteria and definition that SSG will use to determine whether a funding arrangement is abusive.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This could help ensure that the powers given to SSG are being used fairly and consistently and reduce the risk of abuse by providing clear guidance on what constitutes an abusive funding arrangement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Another suggestion would be to provide more oversight and accountability in the enforcement process.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This could be achieved through the establishment of an independent body that is responsible for reviewing and approving enforcement actions, as well as providing guidance as how they should be carried out.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This would provide an independent and impartial source of oversight and help to build trust in the system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This could include providing legal assistance or educational resources to help them understand and comply with the new rules.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   In conclusion, the proposed amendments to the SSG Act and SDL Act are necessary to address fraud and abuse of the SSG funding scheme.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, it is important for SSG to ensure that these amendments are implemented in a fair and transparent manner and take into account the concerns and needs of small businesses.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By addressing these issues, SSG can help to ensure that its funding schemes are used effectively and efficiently to support the skills development of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I would like to take this opportunity to encourage everyone who have not used their Skills Future credits to start considering courses that they may be interested in, be it to upgrade themselves or their skills.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If this Bill is passed, I hope it will give greater confidence to Singaporeans and reduce any doubts about registering for a course to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I have a few questions and some suggestions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In a recent speech at the Singapore Perspectives 2023 Conference, the Minister for Education highlighted how we needed to better support Singaporeans in their lifelong learning ambitions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lifelong learning ensures that our workforce stays productive, adapts to fast-changing global and industrial changes and becomes more resilient in both employment and employability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Singapore's movement towards lifelong learning must be underpinned by assurance that our training institutions are credible.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What type of training would be provided to those officers who are assigned these powers, and what sort of safeguards will be put in place to ensure that these new powers will be used appropriately and not be abused?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When entering a premise against the will of the premise owners, the officers may face hostile resistance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Officers should therefore be adequately trained to exercise their new powers and the requisite rules of engagement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, we need to regularly review and remove courses that have poor enrolment figures to free up funding for courses that Singaporeans actually need and want.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should also regularly review training providers for the conduct of their SSG-funded courses and the effectiveness of these courses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Does SSG require and take into consideration participants' post-course feedback?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I feel that only by holding courses and training providers to a high bar can we attract more Singaporeans to use their SkillsFuture Credits purposefully for training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Work-From-Anywhere trend has meant that more Singaporeans are working remotely even if the work is done for a local company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should move away from funding classes that are held in-person and explore extending more funding to online courses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us support all Singaporeans, regardless of where they are based in their lifelong learning journey.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we work to improve the governance of our lifelong learning funding, we should also ensure that we support the changing aspirations of Singaporeans, as we continue to encourage every Singaporean to be a lifelong learner.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Thus far, it has served Singaporeans well in helping individuals make well-informed choices in education, training and in their careers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Ongoing efforts in maintaining and developing a high-quality education and training system ensure a responsive and relevant resource for the industry and its future developments.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This system must be a platform that can give employers confidence that the skills and training are practical and recognised by the industry, becoming a trusted system for acquiring skills and mastery of capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Above all, it must foster a culture that supports and celebrates lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The main objective is to provide Singaporeans with opportunities to develop their fullest potential throughout their life, regardless of their starting point.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And no matter at which phase in life, one will have access to the resources to attain the skills and training required to be more effective at work and progress further in their career, for some, a less difficult transition into a new industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The integrity, credibility and quality of the system underpin these core tenets.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Of late, the rise of abuse cases has threatened these.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These are growing concerns, and it affects the credibility SkillsFuture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Therefore, it is timely to review the SSG Act to uphold the integrity and the reputation of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: First, how are the penalties ascertained, and how will they evolve?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Given the expanded scope, how do we ensure that the Statutory Board can adhere to high standards of conduct?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How does SSG plan to raise, train and sustain this capability?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Are there any precedents of such expanded powers in other Government Statutory Boards?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Whilst under investigation, will there be powers to impose or lift any interim restrictions imposed on the companies or individuals?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we ensure the process is swift and reasonable during the investigation to avoid unnecessary disruptions?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The various points raised reflect our common interest in strengthening the SkillsFuture movement and equipping Singaporeans with the skills to seize the opportunities ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I would also like to thank Members for their various suggestions on matters such as tapping more on private training providers and companies for upskilling, accreditation of adult educators, types of training to support and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continually review our policies and take Members' suggestions into consideration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will not be addressing them today as they are not directly related to the Bills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I invite Members who would like to have a full reply on these issues to file Parliamentary Questions, so that we can address them properly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, why there is a need for these amendments?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Second, how the amendments will be operationalised, including how the offence and enforcement provisions will work in practice?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Third, whether the penalties and powers of SSG are appropriately calibrated, and whether there are adequate safeguards against abuse?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will address each of these in turn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and several Members talked about the importance of giving Singaporeans the confidence to participate in training programmes of good quality, while Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked whether the amendments are born out of an abundance of caution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, the SkillsFuture movement has been growing steadily in strength.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are continuously strengthening the quality of the Continuing Education and Training (CET) ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The amendments that we are making today will equip SSG with the necessary powers to take action against errant parties who mislead others or abuse SSG's funding system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I would characterise them as part of our ongoing efforts to enhance our system, which has grown steadily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Faced with a wide array of training programmes, Ms Denise Phua, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Don Wee and Mr Melvin Yong have asked about how the public can verify the authenticity of programmes and provide feedback to raise the quality of the courses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The list of SSG-supported courses can be found on the MySkillsFuture portal and can serve as a reference for members of the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Feedback on SSG-funded courses is also taken seriously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Trainees who have undergone training programmes are invited to submit their post-course feedback via the Training Quality and Outcome Measurement, or TRAQOM survey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The results go toward SSG's evaluation of programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The trainees' feedback will also reflect as ratings on the course listing within the portal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Through this effort, we enable learners, companies and bona fide training providers to have greater confidence to participate fully in the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While SSG uses a range of tools to identify advertisements that could be false or misleading, members of the public may contact SSG directly as well if they have doubts about the claims made about SSG-funded programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I urge learners to take ownership of their learning journey, make good use of the available channels to give feedback to SSG on their learning and also point out suspect practices so that collectively we can strengthen our CET ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Sharael Taha asked whether the amendments we are making today will address the underpayment of the SDL owed to SSG.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To clarify, this set of amendments seeks to strengthen SSG's legislative levers and enforcement powers against abuses of SSG's funding system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It has also reviewed its processes to resolve future payment issues in a more scalable and timely manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Sharael Taha also asked about the overpayment of grants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG's plans to streamline its business rules and use more data-at-source verifications and systems-enabled checks, to avoid future lapses, are progressively being implemented.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Allow me to now turn to questions about how the amendments, such as the offence provisions, will be operationalised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether taking legal action can be the last resort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG appreciates that there are administrative errors and missed deadlines that can occur from time to time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These are not regarded as offences, but areas of improvement to be worked on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the outcome of the 93 training providers that SSG had taken action against in 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Actually, the majority of these cases were related to breaches of SSG's funding terms and conditions, such as failing to submit the required annual returns to SSG.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Since these are administrative lapses, most of the 93 training providers were suspended from SSG funding for six months, without further repercussions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In cases such as the publication or distribution of misleading advertisements, opportunity will be given for the errant party to take corrective action, for example, to take down or correct the advertisement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, if the facts of a case constitute an offence, or if there are recalcitrant persons who refuse to comply with SSG's directions, SSG will have to refer the case to AGC to determine the next course of action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked who would be held liable for offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Where the person who commits an offence is an entity, the existing SSG Act and SDL Act already contain provisions which explain the circumstances in which individuals can also be liable for the same offence committed by an entity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, under section 61 of the SSG Act, a director or manager of the company who conspired with others to effect the commission of the offence, may also be guilty of the same offence as the company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked whether the onus to ensure accuracy is on the advertising agency or the training provider.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Mark Chay asked whether the definition of advertisements can include what is communicated to potential learners at roadshows.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The provision covers advertising materials that are distributed at roadshows.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the presumption of intention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As I mentioned in the opening speech, there are three elements to the offence of entering into or facilitating an abusive funding arrangement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, the offenders must have entered into or facilitated an abusive funding arrangement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Second, they must have known, or have had reason to believe, that the funding arrangement is abusive in nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is therefore open to the person to rebut the presumption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Court will consider all the evidence in deciding whether there is intent and whether all the other elements of the offence are present.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will also add that a statutory presumption is not novel and is also found in other similar offences, such as the offence of promoting abusive funding arrangements through the Productivity and Innovation Credit Scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Several members highlighted the need to clearly communicate the changes to training providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG has existing channels of communications with training providers, including circulars, engagements and feedback channels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG intends to have dedicated sessions to explain to training providers the intent and substance of the amendments, and engage them on any clarifications they might have.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will do our best to communicate these changes, but the onus rests with training providers to ensure that they, their partners and their staff adhere to the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how long it would take for SSG to complete investigations for possible offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The length of investigation depends on the scope, complexity of the issue and the level of cooperation received by the involved parties in the investigation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Nonetheless, I assure Members that SSG will take swift and timely action in its investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Following the commencement of the Amendments, SSG will also review the offences to see which ones may be compoundable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On whether recalcitrant companies will be barred or blacklisted, SSG takes a serious view of SSG-funded training providers that do not comply with prevailing regulations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The enforcement actions taken against these errant training providers are published on the Training Partners Gateway portal today, including suspension and termination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Mr Sharael Taha asked about the extra financial expenditure arising from the Amendments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Together with MOE, SSG evaluates its manpower and resourcing requirements on a regular basis to ensure that it is adequately resourced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will consider the Amendments as part of this regular review and ensure that SSG is adequately resourced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Don Wee asked whether SSG would obtain feedback from participants on learning outcomes during investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As I mentioned earlier, SSG collects feedback on learning outcomes comprehensively and also regularly, from trainees via post-training surveys; immediately after the course is completed, and six months after course completion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Such feedback is to monitor quality and guide the CET sector on how we can improve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, I will not preclude investigators using such feedback, or indeed any other available data, if they are relevant to the cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Mark Chay and several Members asked about SSG-appointed inspectors, including whether their powers are appropriate, whether there are safeguards to prevent abuse of power and whether the inspectors have the necessary capabilities to carry out their work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The enhanced investigative powers in the SSG Act are similar to those that SSG currently has and exercises to investigate offences under the Private Education Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There is a robust process to appoint only a selected group of SSG officers as inspectors to exercise powers to investigate offences and their tenure will be subject to regular review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To ensure that inspectors have the necessary and up-to-date skills, they undergo capability development programmes regularly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG officers are trained to leverage technologies and use tools such as data analytics to spot anomalous patterns in support of the enforcement work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG also participates in the regular inter-agency forum where public agencies such as the Police share best practices and experiences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The legislative amendments include safeguards against the abuse of these powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In addition, powers to require the attendance of a person by written order can only be exercised if the inspector has information that the person appears to be acquainted with the case.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Inspectors who abused their powers would be subjected to disciplinary action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The differentiation of roles between authorised persons and inspectors, which Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about, is another safeguard to prevent abuse of power.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The role of authorised persons is to verify information provided by persons who apply for funding from SSG and whether the funds obtained have been properly applied.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On the other hand, inspectors require stronger powers as their role is to investigate offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Because their roles are different, we have differentiated the powers that they can exercise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked whether inspectors can access information stored in the cloud.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For the purpose of investigating an offence under the SSG Act, inspectors have the powers to require any person to provide or grant access, without charge, to electronic documents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Shawn Huang and Ms Denise Phua asked about how penalties are ascertained and whether they are commensurate with the offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As for how the limits are determined, we have referenced the penalties for offences in other Acts to ensure that the penalties in the Bill are appropriate and proportionate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To be clear, it is the Court that determines whether to convict a person of the offence and the penalties to be imposed on a convicted person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As for other enforcement actions that SSG can take, such as taking down a false advertisement, we assess that it is not necessary to have an independent body.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, we have taken concrete steps to enhance the relevance and quality of adult training and education in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Confidence and trust in the training ecosystem have grown, with more individuals participating in upskilling and more companies, trade associations, sector agencies and unions leaning forward to partner SSG to drive skills development in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We must and will continue on this path to strengthen our lifelong learning system, involve industry more closely and encourage innovation, and quality in our training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The two Bills will help enable us to do so in three main ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, by allowing SSG to take legal action against errant parties and achieve a stronger deterrence effect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Second, by protecting learners from being misled into courses through false or misleading advertisements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Third, by enabling the timely and proper restitution of public funds, which ensures that investments from all our stakeholders be it the Government, individual learners, or employers, can be put to good use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: My final point is that building a strong continuing education and training ecosystem is a shared responsibility with learners, enterprises, training providers and the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Through partnerships with the stakeholders, I am confident that we can collectively strengthen the SkillsFuture movement and enable more Singaporeans to acquire the skills that they need, to seize the opportunities ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With this, Mr Speaker, I hope that I have addressed Members' questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And with your permission, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: SSG is also the appointed agency to administer the SDL Act and the Private Education Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To support the skills development of the Singapore workforce, SSG draws on various Government funds, including the Lifelong Learning Endowment Fund (LLEF), the National Productivity Fund (NPF) and the Skills Development Fund (SDF).

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In particular, the SDF, which is one of SSG's main funding sources, comes from the SDL collected from employers for all employees wholly or partly working in Singapore, as required by the SDL Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: SDL collections are channelled into the SDF to support individuals and employers to upskill themselves and their employees respectively.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Continuing Education and Training (CET) landscape in Singapore has evolved over the years.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: More Singaporeans and employers are participating in upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government's investment in CET has also increased significantly.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Hence, it is timely to review the SSG and SDL Acts to put in place tighter mechanisms to protect against the potential abuse of funds provided by SSG, as well as misrepresentation of SSG's funding and SSG-funded courses while ensuring that we continue to support individuals, employers and training providers to further the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: With the substantial increase in Government investments in CET, the risk of abuse of SSG funding has risen correspondingly.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: SSG has come across advertisements that contain false or misleading descriptions about SSG's funding schemes, SSG-funded training courses or SSG-funded training providers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Against this backdrop, there are two key gaps to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: First, the SSG Act currently has limited provisions to deal specifically with the abuse of SSG funding.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Today, SSG can recover wrongly obtained funds through contractual and civil actions.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But recovering funds through civil action can be costly and time consuming.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: More importantly, it does not effectively deter potential abusers from trying to wrongly obtain funds for purposes other than what they are intended for.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Legislative levers to deal with funding abuse cases are thus required.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: However, today, only funding abuse cases that involve the provision of false or misleading information are covered under the existing provisions of the SSG Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Beyond this, SSG will have to rely on the Penal Code to prosecute egregious cases of cheating.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It is necessary to expand the set of offences regulated under the SSG Act to comprehensively and clearly cover the different forms of funding abuse that may arise.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Second, SSG's levers to deal with false or misleading advertisements are limited today.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: When SSG detects these cases, SSG relies on contractual levers to terminate the errant entity's status as an approved training provider, preventing them from offering SSG-subsidised courses further.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: However, SSG does not have legislative levers to direct errant entities to take remedial actions, such as to take down or correct these advertisements.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: If there is continued misrepresentation of SSG's funding schemes and its funded courses, the public could be misled into signing up for unsuitable courses, wasting their resources and effort.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This could undermine public confidence in the broader SkillsFuture movement, to the detriment of other training providers as well.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These new offences will make the SSG Act a more comprehensive piece of legislation to deal with the range of criminal conduct that SSG needs to regulate.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I will now highlight the key features of these new offences and their related provisions inserted by clauses 12 and 13 of the SSG (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Clause 12 also inserts section 57C to set out a specific offence for entering into or facilitating an abusive funding arrangement.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In addition, the Court may order the convicted offender to return the wrongly obtained funds to SSG so that the funds can be used for their intended purposes.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: A past example of an abusive funding arrangement that is not covered by the current SSG Act was where training providers colluded with several companies to apply for grants from SSG.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Individuals were recruited to be employees for the sole purpose of attending a course and drawing training grants from SSG.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The individuals' employment was terminated after the course.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: With the proposed amendments, such abuses will be covered and, hopefully, deterred.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It also includes an advertisement that falsely represents the contents or skill sets that would be acquired through attending an SSG-funded course.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The definitions are based on actual cases of misrepresentations that SSG has encountered.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For example, courses were advertised to be funded by SSG, accredited under the Singapore Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) credentials or would lead to a government-issued diploma when they are not.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This misleads individuals into signing up for unsuitable courses.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: If left unaddressed, such misrepresentations could undermine public confidence in the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Those who are guilty of this offence will be liable for a fine and/or imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We also intend to give SSG powers to direct remedial actions under the new section 57F in the SSG Act as inserted by clause 12.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: SSG can direct remedial actions if it assesses a person has published or distributed such false or misleading advertisement; or caused them to be published or distributed.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Examples of appropriate remedial actions include removing the false and misleading advertisement and publishing a corrective advertisement as approved by SSG.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Under sections 57F and 57G, failure to comply with these directions will be an offence.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Those who are guilty of this offence will be liable for a fine and/or imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Lastly, providing false or misleading information for the purpose of obtaining SSG funding is currently an offence under section 58 of the SSG Act and those convicted of the offence are liable for a fine and/or imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: However, SSG currently has to rely on contractual levers and civil proceedings to recover the funds that have been wrongly obtained as a result of such false or misleading information.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: At this juncture, I would like to make it clear that our intention is not to penalise administrative lapses or genuine mistakes of the training providers that could occur from time to time.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: However, if the facts of a case constitute an offence, SSG will have to refer the case to AGC to determine the appropriate course of action.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: By safeguarding those that are genuine in the pursuit of training, we hope to create a vibrant CET ecosystem of quality training providers and programmes, where companies and individuals participate in and will benefit from skills upgrading.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Further, I would like to assure Members that there will be due process where SSG exercises these expanded regulatory powers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For example, before directing a person to remove an advertisement, or to refund trainees or SSG if the course is cancelled, SSG will first give a written notice for the person to submit written representations to explain their actions unless it is not practicable or desirable within a reasonable specified timeline.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: SSG will decide whether to issue the direction or to modify it after considering the written representation by the person.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: If a person is aggrieved by SSG's direction, the person can appeal to the Minister.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Clause 12 will insert section 57H to provide for this.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In view of the new offences, SSG's enforcement powers will need to be enhanced.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Under the SSG Act today, SSG's enforcement powers are for limited purposes, mainly to verify information submitted to SSG for SSG funding, as well as to ensure that SSG funding had been properly applied by the funding recipient.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Persons authorised by SSG may enter premises, take photos and videos, access documents and ask for returns within a specified period.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: However, these powers are limited and are not sufficient for the investigation of offences.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To provide SSG with stronger levers to investigate offences under the SSG Act, clause 12 of the SSG (Amendment) Bill enhances SSG's enforcement powers by inserting the new section 57A to empower SSG-appointed inspectors to verify identities of persons reasonably believed to have committed the offence, require attendance, conduct interviews and, where necessary, search for and seize documents or equipment for the purpose of investigating offences under the SSG Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These powers are largely similar to the ones that SSG has currently under the Private Education Act, where SSG-appointed inspectors are already equipped to investigate offences under the Act, such as publishing false or misleading advertisements.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Clause 9 of the SDL (Amendment) Bill will amend the SDL Act to confer on SSG-appointed inspectors similar enforcement powers for the purpose of investigation of offences relating to SDL.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will also take this opportunity to make other amendments to streamline operational processes within the SSG Act and the SDL Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Currently, offences and enforcement powers relating to incentives, grants or loans are set out in the SDL Act or SSG Act, depending on whether the funding source is SDF monies or non-SDF monies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Clause 6 of the SDL (Amendment) Bill repeals the offence and related provisions concerning SSG funding out of SDF monies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Offences and enforcement powers that pertain to the levy will remain in the SDL Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Second, we will make it easier for employers to compute SDL liabilities and make monthly contributions for both Central Provident Fund (CPF) and SDL.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Today, employers use the definition of "wages" under the CPF Act, to calculate the CPF payable for their local employees, and a slightly different definition of "remuneration" to compute the SDL payable for their employees.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For example, certain medical benefits are currently considered part of "remuneration" but not part of "wages" and, therefore, subject to SDL and not CPF.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This can result in additional administrative burden on employers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We currently intend for employers to adopt the same definition in the CPF Act of what constitutes wages, before applying the respective formulas to compute SDL payable.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government's continued investment in SkillsFuture is critical, given that lifelong learning and employability is a new pillar under our social compact.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: With the increasing pace of change in industries and jobs brought about by automation and digitalisation, we must continue to prepare the Singapore workforce for the future economy.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To do so, we need to strengthen the quality of the training and adult education ecosystem, including stepping up our legislative levers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The new offences and related provisions in the Bills seek to enable SSG to better deter and take appropriate actions against abuse of funding given by SSG and misrepresentation of SSG's schemes.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This will allow individuals and employers to have greater confidence to participate in training.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will also better protect genuine learners from being misled into taking courses that are of little or no value.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This will also benefit the majority of training providers who are bona fide in their commitment to workforce training and skills development.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The enhanced measures will also help ensure that investments from the Government, individuals, employers and other stakeholders will be channelled towards legitimate training providers and courses and put to their intended use.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Together, these moves will strengthen the SkillsFuture movement and support our effort to equip Singaporeans with the skills needed to seize the opportunities ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I rise in support of these amendment Bills to strengthen SSG's regulatory powers, but I am highlighting the need for robust safeguards in place to prevent abuse of power and to ensure the continued vital role of private training providers and CET centres in lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Two, marketing agents soliciting sign-ups without intention to offer a course and submitting claims without the individuals' knowledge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Three, collusion involving multiple companies, where claims were submitted to SSG for disguised "employees" whose only role was to attend SSG-funded courses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At present, SSG has some avenues of recourse to act against those who abuse SSG funding, those who misrepresent SSG and to verify information submitted for fund application and fund usage.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, one, SSG can take legal and civil actions against errant training providers who abuse SSG funding but there are limitations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Cases that constitute a cheating offence under the Penal Code can be referred to the Police for investigation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, not all cases of training grant abuse can constitute an offence as defined under the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are also not covered by current offences under the SSG Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For these cases, SSG does have the option to terminate funding and recover wrongfully disbursed funds through civil action.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Civil action however does not effectively deter training providers, companies and individuals who are all out to abuse the system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Two, SSG can use contractual levers to take action against errant training providers who misrepresent SSG-approved funding courses and funding information, but they can be difficult to enforce in practice and insufficient in deterrence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: From time to time, SSG encounters cases involving misrepresentation of SSG-approved courses or funding information.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These include falsely indicating that the course is recognised by the Government, falsely indicating that a course is free when, in reality, SkillsFuture Credits is needed to be used or even false promises of obtaining nationally recognised qualifications upon course completion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While contractual levers such as terminating funding and approved status of delinquent training providers can be used, SSG lacks the legislative levers to direct errant training providers to take remedial actions, such as refunding out-of-pocket course fees paid by trainees or repaying subsidies obtained from SSG.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A concern here is that the continued misrepresentation of SSG's funding schemes could mislead the public into signing up for unsuitable courses and undermine public confidence in our lifelong learning ecosystem and how SSG is using its funds to drive the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Three, SSG officers have the powers to verify information submitted for fund application and usage, but they are intended for routine inquiries only.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The current SSG Act gives SSG officers powers to verify information provided by a person who applies for SSG funding and whether the funding has been used properly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, these powers are intended for routine inquiries to verify information collected and ensure funds are used properly, and are not sufficient to investigate funding abuse cases, especially those that are more elaborately concealed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is definitely a pressing need for these greater powers to be bestowed on SSG to investigate and prosecute as we weed out abuses by training providers, and in particular, the "black sheep" which we have seen in past years when SkillsFuture and other training funding schemes were meant to encourage individual-initiated training, company-supported training and lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, we do not want to dampen the important role which private training providers play in the training, transformation and lifelong learning ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As such, even as SSG is given greater powers, I further submit that we need the four "Cs" – of communication, clarity, credentials and contemporaneity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I call for the creation of additional modes and levels of communication and clarification between SSG and our training providers before a direction is issued to facilitate a cooperative relationship between training providers and SSG, relegating the issuance of directions for remedial actions only as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Additionally, there should be in place proper public and training provider communications on these new set of powers including frequently asked questions (FAQs) and detailed illustrations in a simple-to-read format.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A clearer explanation and breakdown that is simple and easily accessible to training providers on what constitutes an "abusive funding arrangement" and "misleading information" should be provided.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I ask for further specifications of the credentials of those who will be appointed as SSG inspectors and whether they will be staff who are trained and equipped to carry out such investigative and enforcement work, or whether this role will be outsourced, out of SSG?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And, since SSG inspectors and officers are also now exempt from personal liability as per their inclusion in section 42, how will accountability be established in the case of abuse of powers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I ask this as training providers may be suspended and kept hanging in the air while waiting for investigations to be carried out.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I support the expanded scope of powers given to SSG-appointed inspectors, but opine that it is imperative to have the robust safeguards in place such that these powers are not abused.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As someone who had previously sought clarifications on lapses identified by the Auditor-General's Office (AGO) for SkillsFuture grants, I agree with the revisions embedded in these two Acts, the aim to plug gaps in the framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My comments today will first focus, however, on offering some constructive critique on the stipulations in the respective Bills including the benefits, but also what I regard as minor shortcomings that remain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will go on to ask a meta-question, whether the proposed regulatory enhancements alone are sufficient to ensure that SSG is able to identify and ensure the training providers for our workers are the very best available.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The proposed measures that lend greater agency to SSG to investigate potential abuses of SSG grants and additional authority to pursue external providers that engage in fraudulent or predatory practices are sound.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 12 of the Bill embodies a type of clawback provision, beyond fines, per se.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This distinction is important, because channelling recovered monies toward funding operational costs, which I believe is what clause 9 allows, may strike one as a pragmatic way to finance the agency tasked with oversight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in my view, there is one downside from such an approach, which I hope SSG will guard against.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tying enforcement actions to funding can give rise to potentially perverse incentives toward zealous or over-regulation and possible abuse by state authorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has been the case with asset seizure and civil forfeiture laws in the United States, which, in the most egregious cases, have given rise to predatory police misbehaviour, excessive punishments and the erosion of due process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In August last year, I, along with others, had filed queries based on the AGO report about how identified overpayments would be recovered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Minister Chan's written response at the time was that and I quote, "lapses… were primarily due to wrong declarations by the grant applicants and errors in manual processing of grants".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This conveys the notion that there had not been much gaming of the system, and that most disbursements were simply due to idiosyncratic human error.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In an oral response to other Members of this House – including my Workers' Party colleague, Ms Sylvia Lim – Ms Gan went on to elaborate that the bulk of these errors had occurred, "prior to November 2020, when SSG's previous IT system… had used a declaration-based approach".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, however, one is left wondering if SSG misappropriations are the result of genuine errors which are relatively small, and probably, a matter of the past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While, of course, no misappropriation of public monies should be deemed acceptable, one is led to wonder if the Ministry currently regards the sort of abuses that the Bill seeks to address as a chronic and worrisome issue, or if the safeguards introduced are more out of an abundance of caution and prudence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, may I ask the Ministry to elaborate on how it currently tracks such abuses?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By this, I mean, how SSG goes beyond internal and external audits of grant disbursements, per se, to how it goes about evaluating where the progress proposed by training providers meet not just their stated objectives but contribute toward genuine, economically valuable skills acquisition, and how subpar performance may be assessed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, the new sections 57E and F introduced by the Bill allow for the policing of false or misleading advertising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what if there is collusion between a given provider and trainee or trainees, where a provider receives the funds, shares the proceeds with the trainees and skips delivery of the training?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What if the courses offered appear to be associated more with consumption – home decoration or flower arrangement or wine tasting – rather than evidently future-relevant skills, which presumably is the purpose of the agency?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will return to this second concern later in my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Ministry assures us that, in practice, employers are already doing so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The concern here is that, were this realignment to come to pass, such wages then go on to become part of the earned income of SkillsFuture recipients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
