text: More specifically, I am concerned if the changes proposed by clause 2 will be limited to just the manner by which employers file SDL, or will the SDL amounts also be included into total compensation for employees?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, I can imagine how doing so may result in an unintended consequence of discouraging the use of SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many Government subsidy programmes are pegged to total compensation, and if SkillsFuture credits become recognised as another component of this mix, this may unintentionally lead workers to forgo training, to ensure that they fall below some income threshold that qualifies them for a higher tier of subsidy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, I had recently appealed for a resident who, having received an IT device allowance to assist with the transition to work-from-home arrangements, found herself inadvertently and unwillingly bumped into a higher income threshold, thereby qualifying for lower subsidies, as a result.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The last thing we would want is for SkillsFuture, which is made for investment in one's human capital, to become perceived as an undesirable component of total income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Providers, in turn, could focus on course content and delivery, rather than be pressed with identifying and locating students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This specialisation can, therefore, improve the overall efficiency of the SkillsFuture ecosystem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, for the system to work and operate well, it is key that the courses are adapted to the needs of both the future economy, as well as those of firms seeking skilled workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presumably, this means that SSG will have done its homework in being in conversation with employers, to ensure that certified courses and competencies do indeed match the needs of industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Minister Chan has stated in the past that SSG will make efforts to encourage the development of skills in future-oriented sectors, such as the green, care and digital economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would only add that the agency should not apply a blanket ban but consider the context as each case may present itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While my suggestion that flower arrangement or wine tasting could be regarded as forms of consumption, and perhaps, frivolous consumption, they could well become spinoffs into viable businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We do not wish to stamp out the entrepreneurial spirits that could launch the next Edible Arrangements or Coravin.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, at the same time, we should not neglect the other elements of the supply side.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is essential that the pool of external providers be kept as large as possible, even as the set of courses eligible for funding narrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, while it is crucial to ensure that trainers are indeed qualified to deliver the courses they offer, accreditation as a SkillsFuture provider should not conversely be too onerous, so as not to otherwise discourage legitimate trainers and courses from becoming part of that pool.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, this has not been my impression of the manner by which SkillsFuture currently recognises training providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One example is how difficult it is for individual educators to qualify and become an approved training provider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, as Members of this House are aware, I declare that I am, of course, an educator myself, working at a private tertiary educational institution in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Training professionals are required to secure an Advanced Certificate in Learning and Performance (ACLP).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, asking experienced educators, such as university professors or tertiary education instructors, to go through additional pedagogical training is a severe impediment to their involvement, not least given the extensive demands already on the time of such professionals, who juggle a slate of existing teaching, research and service commitments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The last thing we wish to do is to burden them with so-called "busy work", which would diminish their incentives to participate as a training provider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But also, for a moment, imagine asking an academic from one of our world-class universities, which may be one of subject-matter experts in the world, to sit through months of classes, just so that they may have the privilege of offering education to our continuing education students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question that I filed about this approach, Minister Chan indicated that "adults with prior relevant experience can seek credit exemption… if they have comparable TAE qualifications and can provide evidence of relevant practice and experience." But such exemptions tend to be based on other comparable adult education qualifications and there is little indication on the Institute of Adult Learning site that experience alone, coupled with domain-specific expertise, which tends to be the case for many university professors, would itself be sufficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the revised ACLP 2.0 does not seem to offer any credit exemptions, perhaps due to its novelty and already truncated nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: University educators are not the only ones constrained by the current set-up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that only 10% of SSG-funded courses were previously performed in-house.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Was the scheme cancelled then due to perceived lack of interest?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, it would strike me as strange to wind down funding for in-house training based on this statistic alone, rather than seeking to further promote take-up, because there is evidence that such in-house training can be particularly effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Member Mr Raj Joshua Thomas had asked in this House about how apprenticeships would be accredited, and Minister Chan's response was that the "Workforce Skills Qualification (WSQ) Framework includes an Assessment-Only Pathway (AOP)… and is available across more than 500 courses".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this is wonderful, but it remains unclear the extent to which the WSQ AOP is being utilised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In addition, the assessment of the WSQ competency standards still comes across as extremely academic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I am fully aware of the irony of this observation, coming from an actual academic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, while ensuring minimum standards are surely necessary, do we want journeymen and master skillsmen to subject themselves to curriculum design and development, or painstakingly document pedagogical objectives for each and every lesson, rather than to actually go about teaching the craft?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Are we subjecting them to knowledge assessment questions that test whether they are able to recall, and this is from the actual literature, what "three types of food contaminants" are, or if they can "list four unhygienic personal habits", to the detriment of chefs who genuinely possess the creativity and skills to helm Michelin-starred restaurants?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The entire purpose of an apprenticeship scheme is to allow those who are less likely to excel in acquiring paper qualifications to demonstrate their abilities by doing, rather than knowing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, while there is certainly some value in having such pedagogical tools weaved in, continuity after staff turnover, ensuring coverage of critical concepts, I would go so far as to argue that these should be defined only at a very high level, rather than preoccupy the time of otherwise erstwhile teachers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While these Bills have been focused on the supply side, we also do need to pay some attention to fostering demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I am hopeful that even as we tighten the regulatory constraints to eliminate fraud and abuse of the system, we will also explore ways to reduce the hurdle rate placed on the legitimate training providers, to ensure that the skills imparted on our trainees and mid-career switchers are, indeed, the best available ones for the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The amendments tabled in this Bill are urgent and deserve the full support of the House.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The SSG plays an important role to drive and implement the national SkillsFuture movement, to promote a culture of lifelong learning through skills mastery by the people of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There has been an increasingly complicated developments of abuse of SSG fundings, I guess because of the rapidly expanding and CET market and the seduction of the funds.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Then, there are people, the individuals who submitted false claims without taking any courses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Then, there are some employers are known to falsely submit names of trainees who are not really employees, with the intent to just access SSG grants.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition, some training providers also knowingly market their courses through misrepresentation of information, such as free courses when they are truly not; or untrue learning outcomes and untrue training durations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Persons guilty can be anyone in the value chain of training, it can be training providers, marketing agents, employers, employees and even training participants themselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The issue has to be urgently resolved; lest SSG be wrongly perceived as a toothless agency and abuses and frauds become rampant.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But there is a more important reason, in my view, for quickly resolving this and for our support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Just a few days ago, Education Minister Chan Chun Sing delivered a brilliant public speech on the future of the education landscape of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He said that the first 15 years of one's education are important; but what happens to one's education in the next 50 years will make or break one's future career, and collectively, I believe, Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The adult CET landscape will see further growth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SSG, therefore, cannot afford to spend too much of its attention on fending off abuses and frauds, so that it can direct resources to focus on its core business of designing and delivering lifelong learning nationally.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Notwithstanding my support, I seek clarification for specific provisions of the Bills, most of which are in clause 15, which inserts a new section 57.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the Bill will make it an offence for anyone to enter or facilitate an abusive funding arrangement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My questions are these: one, do the penalties in fines and/or imprisonment commensurate with the size of the offence?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Should there, or ought there be, heavier penalties, as suggested during public consultations?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What interim measures can be taken by SSG whilst potentially long investigations are ongoing?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And in the event that the errant party who is guilty, is an entity, to whom will the punishment be meted – the staff, the management or the director?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, the Bill will make it an offence to knowingly publish or distribute any false or misleading advertisement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Does the onus to ensure accuracy fall on the advertising agency or the content provider?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Should SSG consider the provision of guidelines, rules or templates to better guide training providers, their marketing agents or advertisers in what constitutes acceptable and non-acceptable marketing practices, since prevention is indeed better than cure?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Are there means by which potential trainees can protect themselves, by referring to a repository of SSG-supported courses and information for validation before one registers for courses?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On to the next feature of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill will grant an expanded scope of powers to SSG-appointed inspectors to investigate the added offences and provide for a series of power to do so.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition to that provided in the Bill, do the powers of these inspectors grant them access to information stored, for example, in the cloud, in view of the rise of cloud storage sitting in, perhaps, external parties?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will SSG tap on the use of technology, example: Artificial Intelligence (AI), to detect discrepancies routinely?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And as white-collar crime investigations require a high degree of specialised expertise – how does SSG plan to access this body of expertise?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will SSG groom homegrown forensic experts to carry out this newly expanded scope of duties?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am keen to know when and how the sum of this extra financial expenditure will be determined.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And instead of only budgeting for the capacity and capability needed to carry out the additional regulatory powers of this Bill, I strongly urge SSG to work on the following two pieces of work for its future plan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, to strengthen self-monitoring as a feature of the ecosystem of the landscape.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides a better whistle-blowing practice, for example, SSG should appoint credible training partners, such as National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), or SSG's larger Queen Bee partners, or the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), larger industry partners to assist it, in not just curating or developing training solutions, but also help build systems to strengthen self-monitoring in their respective specific market segments.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another piece of work that I feel is cut out for SSG to do would be to review the SkillsFuture ecosystem for stronger impact.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With more resources expected to come through the education space throughout one's lifespan, SSG cannot afford to do things in the same way.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There must be found better ways to design, organisation and re-allocate resourcing of learning at all ages and levels.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: More dialogues and actions for SSG and its trusted partners to bring the SkillsFuture movement to the next height.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The five Community Development Council (CDCs) are looking forward and ever ready to support SSG also, to help build and develop learning communities at the ground level.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have seen in 2017, a crime syndicate attempted to defraud SSG of nearly $40 million dollars.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In 2018, a human resources (HR) consultancy tried to cheat SSG of $145,000.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, by making changes in the Bills, we can avoid such incidents and ensure that our public resources are used effectively and for their intended purposes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have several clarifications and proposals on the Bills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we can do more to improve the quality of training providers by better taking in feedback from users.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is heartening to hear that there are already different tiers of funding for training providers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Steps are also in place to remove funding and subsidies from courses which are deemed to be non-certifiable, to better fund quality ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government consider setting up a dedicated channel for users to provide feedback to SSG on courses and trainers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, users can provide feedback on courses from the relevance of the courses to their work, to the quality of the trainers and teaching agencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is important because some of my residents in Yio Chu Kang have informed me that they were hesitant to use their SkillsFuture credits, due to a lack of confidence in the quality of available courses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may have heard anecdotal feedback from other students about courses being too basic or impractical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is also no way to seek recourse if the training providers under-deliver or fail to match students' expectations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, I believe the Government can do more to provide better quality assurance for SkillsFuture courses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is so that more Singaporeans are willing to commit their credits, time and energy to these opportunities, at the assurance that they will not be wasted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the Ministry have more recent data on the total utilisation for the year 2022?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we do more to assure Singaporeans that the quality of the SkillsFuture courses is worth spending their time and credits on?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, more clarity is needed on the skills and roles of enforcement personnel.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As enforcement personnel will receive additional investigative powers, where will they receive training in investigative skills?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will we leverage on industry professionals, or the Police, to guide them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Why is there a need for authorised persons and inspectors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While these roles are differentiated by the need for routine versus intrusive investigative powers, could they not be consolidated under the role of the inspector?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, how does the agency identify suitable individuals to be authorised persons or inspectors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have spoken to training providers who are concerned by the presumption of intention created by clause 57C(7).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, I seek clarification as to the mechanics of the presumption, and to understand the rationale behind the necessity of such a presumption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is important as we do not wish to create a chilling effect on legitimate training providers, who may otherwise be deterred because of the presumption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides the IHLs are private training agencies audited every year on both the skills they provide and the claims that they file, who is responsible for ensuring that they do not commit fraud?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is my understanding that, in order to be a Training Provider under SkillsFuture, an organisation must, unless otherwise permitted, be an organisation registered in Singapore with the relevant authorities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What about foreign individuals or organisations who seek to provide training under the SkillsFuture scheme?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, would their qualifications and expertise be subject to authentication or evaluation, in order to ensure that they meet the necessary standards for providing training?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we must also consider escalating the penalties and enforcement efforts for those who abuse SkillsFuture funding or breach its terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support the higher penalties recommended in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry provide more information on the outcomes of these actions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we use this experience to better calibrate the severity of the new penalties and to safeguard our public monies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition to increasing penalties, will the Ministry consider barring recalcitrant companies and their respective officers and creating a blacklist of companies with major infractions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should also consider having a whitelist of companies that are seen as role models in the industry, to make it easier for residents to choose a trusted provider.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is despite efforts to effect collection from 2015 to 2020.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does this Bill ensure that SSG is able to improve the enforcement of recovering owed payments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, what steps have been taken to address this gap in enforcement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Enforcement of judgement debt in the Civil Court would incur time and costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would also be subject to the nuances of the various enforcement methods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even as we are coming out of the pandemic, we are seeing major nations engaging in big power contestations, both in the East and in the West.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We would not have anticipated today's events, say five to 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: All these uncertainties and insecurities have major implications on important issues, such as trade and digital connectivity and on our place in the world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One undeniable response to the macro environment must be to evolve our education system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a country with no natural resources, Singaporeans continue to be Singapore's best asset.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that our education system delivers and continues to deliver for the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our citizens must continue to engage in lifelong learning and respond to the larger environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It requires the individual to be inquisitive, resilient, have an open mind and go outside his comfort zone to master new skillsets relevant for the new environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And this is an unremitting process – learning, unlearning and sometimes, relearning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Often times, it requires sacrifice of time and effort.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I was doing one of my Masters, I remember going off work at 6.30 pm to travel from my workplace at Buona Vista to Jalan Bahar to attend financial engineering classes at Nanyang Technological University (NTU) and returning to office at 11.00 pm to finish up work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This happened two times a week, for close to two years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It has opened my mind to new knowledge and value, and has helped me develop new competences to take up different responsibilities in my career.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A robust education system will prepare our people to learn for life.
